content: Rifampin may interfere with the elimination of certain chemicals used in gallbladder tests, potentially affecting test results. In the event of an overdose, if someone experiences severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center promptly. U.S. residents can reach the poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Before starting this medication and during its use, your doctor may order laboratory tests, such as liver and kidney function tests, bilirubin levels, and a complete blood count, to monitor your health. It is essential to attend all medical and laboratory appointments as scheduled. This medication is prescribed specifically for your current condition and should not be used for other purposes. If you miss a dose, consult your doctor or pharmacist immediately to establish a new dosing schedule. Proper storage of this medication is crucial; follow the product instructions and consult your pharmacist for details. Do not dispose of medications by flushing them down the toilet or pouring them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Discard this product appropriately when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about this medication. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or suitable for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information tailored to your specific health needs. Rifampin is used to prevent and treat tuberculosis and other bacterial infections. It belongs to a class of drugs called rifamycin antibiotics and is effective only against bacterial infections. It does not work for viral infections, such as the common cold or flu. This medication is administered by injection into a vein, typically once or twice daily, as directed by your doctor. Before use, visually inspect the product for particles or discoloration; do not use it if either is present. It is critical to continue using this medication, along with other prescribed tuberculosis treatments, exactly as directed by your doctor. For optimal effectiveness, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals and complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, nausea, or headache. Rifampin may also cause harmless discoloration of urine, sweat, saliva, or tears (yellow, orange, red, or brown), which will resolve once the medication is stopped. Remember, this medication is prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, rifampin may cause serious, potentially fatal liver disease. It may also lead to a severe intestinal condition caused by the bacteria Clostridium difficile (C. diff), which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Additionally, it may sometimes result in oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Severe allergic reactions to this drug are rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for guidance. Before using rifampin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other rifamycins (e.g., rifabutin), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Avoid alcohol, as it may increase the risk of liver disease. Rifampin may reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine). During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly necessary. If used in the last few weeks of pregnancy, it may increase the risk of bleeding in both the mother and infant. Notify your doctor immediately if you observe any bleeding in your newborn. Rifampin passes into breast milk but is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription, non-prescription, and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Rifampin interacts with many medications and can accelerate the removal of other drugs from your body, potentially affecting their effectiveness. It may also reduce the efficacy of hormonal birth control methods (e.g., pills, patches, or rings), increasing the risk of pregnancy. Discuss with your doctor or pharmacist whether you should use reliable backup birth control methods while taking this medication. Rifampin may interfere with certain laboratory tests (e.g., urine screening for opiates, blood serum folate, or vitamin B12), potentially causing false test results. It may also make it more difficult for your body to eliminate certain chemicals used in gallbladder tests.
